beats: The coldest part of a snow cannon isn't the water. It's a puff of air.
Tiny water drops can stay liquid well below zero Celsius, thirty-two Fahrenheit.
To freeze, they need a starting point: a seed of ice to grow on.
So the cannon makes its own seeds, in a small nozzle called the nucleator.
Inside, a little water is mixed with compressed air.
As it leaves the nozzle, the air expands suddenly, and expanding air gets very cold.
The water caught in that blast freezes into specks of ice. Those are the seeds.
Around it, the main nozzles spray much bigger drops.
The fan throws everything high into the cold air, so the drops have time to fall.
On the way down, a seed touches a drop, and the whole drop freezes around it.
That's why machine snow is tiny frozen beads, not flakes.
No puff of air, no seeds, no snow.
